structure.note: Three classes: Class B carries ten votes per share, Class A one vote and Class C none. The FY2024 10-K says Larry Page and Sergey Brin together beneficially owned about 87.4% of Class B, about 52.1% of the voting power, at December 31, 2024. The 2025 proxy gives Page 27.1% and Brin 25.2% of total voting power. No single person holds a majority, so 'controlled' is false, but the two co-founders together do.

ecosystem.notes: Alphabet reports no gross flow volume for its platforms, so measure is null. payouts is TAC: FY2024 TAC was $54.9B. The 10-K defines it as amounts paid to distribution partners (browser providers, mobile carriers, OEMs, software developers) and to Google Network partners. The TAC rate is 20.7% of advertising revenues, as stated in the 10-K. platformRevenue is Google advertising revenues ($264.59B) because TAC is measured against advertising. Total Alphabet revenues were $350.018B. YouTube creator payments are not in TAC. The 10-K puts them inside 'content acquisition costs' in other cost of revenues and gives no separate amount. The YouTube $100B figure is company-reported, covers four years in total (Jan 2021–Dec 2024) and is not an FY2024 flow. Its source URL is on services.google.com, Google's own file host; the records validator's search-page check (/google\./) would wrongly flag it.

economicActivity.label: Economic activity Google helped provide
economicActivity.definition: Google's own estimate of the economic activity that Google Search, Google Ads, Google Cloud, AdSense/AdMob, Ad Grants, YouTube and Google Play helped provide for a state's businesses, nonprofits, publishers, creators and developers. Modeled by the Google Economics team (e.g. $8 of profit per $1 of Google Ads spend), not measured output, not GDP and not Google's own spending. States reported in millions are converted to billions (shown in square brackets in the quote).

businesses.label: Businesses using Google's free tools
businesses.definition: Businesses in the state that "used Google's tools at no cost to receive phone calls, bookings, reviews, requests for directions, or other direct connections to their customers". Always reported as "more than".

investment.label: Cumulative Google investment in the state
investment.period: cumulative, from the year the state's first data center was built through the 2024 report
investment.definition: Google's statement that it "has invested more than" (Georgia: "has committed more than ... of investment") the amount in the state since its data center(s) there were built. Reported only for the 13 states with Google data centers; cumulative, not annual.

longLivedAssets.label: Long-lived assets
longLivedAssets.definition: Property and equipment, net, plus operating lease assets, by geographic area (10-K Note 15). Columns are 2023 then 2024; the 2024 value is recorded.

footprint.notes: Source: Google's own 2024 U.S. Economic Impact Report (national PDF with one page per state, data for calendar 2024, PDF created April 2025), the edition matching the Dec 2024 snapshot. The live site economicimpact.google now shows the 2025 edition (published April 2026, higher figures); not used. Methodology page credits the Google Economics team and its own multipliers (Hal Varian's $2 profit per $1 ad spend, organic-click adjustment), so tier is company-published, not commissioned, but the economic-activity figures are model estimates of value to other businesses, not Google spending. 50 states + DC have economic activity and business counts; Puerto Rico has a page too ($269 million, 141,000+ businesses) but is not a state, so it is left out. Investment figures exist only for the 13 states with data centers and are cumulative since each data center was built. The report also gives philanthropic giving, volunteer hours and Ad Grants by state; not recorded. Google publishes no employees-by-state figures here (nationally: more than 100,000 U.S. full-time employees, offices and data centers in 26 states). The 10-K gives no property breakdown by state or country, so sites are the HQ (10-K) plus 11 data centers as described on the state pages. No employee, office or tax breakdown by country was found; the only geographic split of physical footprint in the 10-K is long-lived assets (property and equipment plus operating lease assets), United States vs International, recorded as one country row and one region row. Google's data-center locations page (google.com/about/datacenters/locations) and office list (about.google/locations) were checked: both are current (2026) lists of places with no figures, so they add nothing countable; the data-center sites above use the 2024 report's own wording. Tier basis: the 2024 PDF's methodology is written in Google's voice ("Our first chief economist, Hal Varian"), with no outside author named.
